messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 36
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tax Consultant
  trauma_type: Military
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Conflict: Confrontations, Certain Conversation Topics: Certain conversation topics, Feeling Ill: Feeling physically unwell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others, Avoid Positive Feelings: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
  Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

The convoy had been moving through a narrow alley in Fallujah when the IED detonated. For Marcus, a 36-year-old tax consultant living in a quiet suburb of Denver, the memory is not a sequence of images but a sensory event. When it returns—and it returns often—he can taste the acrid, metallic dust that filled his mouth as the blast wave threw him against the armored vehicle’s interior. He remembers the silence that followed, a dense, unnatural quiet before the shouting began, and how that silence felt like a held breath before something worse. That specific quality of silence has never left him. Now, years later, when his wife goes quiet during an argument or when the office falls into a lull, Marcus feels his chest tighten. Unusual silence makes him feel something dangerous is about to happen, and he finds himself scanning the room for exits, noting the quickest path to the door before he can even think about what he is doing. He always identifies escape routes before he feels comfortable anywhere, a habit that has become as automatic as breathing.

The memory itself is overwhelming. When it surfaces, usually triggered by an unexpected confrontation or a conversation that veers too close to the war, Marcus feels so flooded with emotion that he has to stop whatever he is doing. He will excuse himself from a meeting, go to the bathroom, and press his palms against the cool tile until the taste of dust fades. But the memory is inconsistent. Sometimes he can recall what happened but feels completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger. That detachment is almost worse, because it makes him feel broken, like a man watching his own life from a distance. He has come to believe that his emotions are dangerous, that feeling anything strongly—even happiness—is a trap. He pushes away positive emotions because they feel unsafe, a conviction that has made him distant from his wife and young daughter. He avoids talking with others about the event or its aftermath, and he has learned to steer conversations away from anything military, anything loud, anything that might pull the memory forward.

The triggers are specific and inescapable. Confrontations at work, even mild disagreements with a client about a tax deduction, feel like an ambush. Certain conversation topics—politics, news from the Middle East, even discussions about safety—send his mind reeling back to the alley. When he feels physically unwell, even a mild headache or an upset stomach, he immediately feels the threat of the memory closing in, as if his body is telling him that something is about to go wrong. In response, he has developed a strategy of avoidance that governs his daily life. He avoids any form of physical contact with others. When a colleague claps him on the shoulder, he reacts with alarm, his body jerking before his mind catches up. He has stopped shaking hands at networking events, a professional liability for a tax consultant who needs to build trust with clients. He has started working from home whenever possible, but even there, the silence of the house can feel threatening. He finds himself planning escape routes in restaurants, in the grocery store, in his own living room.

The cycle is tight and self-reinforcing. The triggers bring the memory, and the memory makes him feel threatened, which makes him hypervigilant to the next trigger. His avoidance strategies—pushing away feelings, avoiding touch, steering conversations—paradoxically make the triggers more potent because he never learns that they are safe. The taste of dust returns when he is stressed, and the stress of avoiding the memory makes the taste more vivid. He has begun to avoid his wife’s touch entirely, and she has started to ask him what is wrong. He cannot tell her. He does not have the words. What finally brought him to seek help was the moment his daughter, age four, reached for his hand and he flinched. He saw her face fall, and he knew that something in him was broken in a way that silence and escape routes could no longer hide. He is terrified that he will lose his family the way he lost his sense of safety, but he is equally afraid that talking about the memory will make it real again, that the taste of dust will never leave his mouth.
